radicals.meaningMnemonic: This looks just like a folding <radical>stool</radical>, am I right?

A leaf growing out of a… mouth?? Look again and see the mouth is actually made of <radical>stone</radical>. The leaf here was just growing out of a crack on the side. Makes this stone mouth sculpture look kinda elegant, if you ask me. And obviously leaves don't grow on mouths, so whenever you see a leaf on a mouth, remember it's gotta be stone.

This radical looks like a <radical>spoon</radical>! Well, a spoon that's been bent a lot by an angry person or a psychic. Go grab a spoon and try to bend it into this shape. Then hold on to it so you'll never forget that this is the spoon radical!

This radical looks just like the katakana character "ra" (ラ). The sound "ra" sounds just like the famous Egyptian God "Ra" as well, so we're going to say this radical represents Egypt's God <radical>Ra</radical>.

This is no ordinary enclosure. It is an enclosure with an extra reinforcement (see it sticking out the bottom right of the enclosure radical?). Why is this enclosure reinforced? Because it's the <radical>raptor cage</radical>. I wonder how long they'll be able to hold the raptors... It didn't work out all that well on Jurassic Park...

This is the radical for <radical>winter</radical>. It looks like a skier going downhill (to the left), with their skis out in front and their poles out behind them. And when do people ski? In winter!

You could also remember this as looking like the evening radical but with an extra long stroke, since the evenings are long in winter. It gets dark early in winter, you know?

This looks like a clothesline pole you would <radical>dry</radical> clothes on. It's got two very straight horizontal poles, for maximum drying efficiency. If you were gonna dry your clothes, you'd dry them on this thing.
This is a <radical>canopy</radical>. See the cloth draping down and the little point at the middle holding it up? You could sit under here and enjoy a bright summer day without getting any sun!

This looks like a long index finger bent at the bottom, with several other stubby fingers growing out of it on either side. That makes it the <radical>fingers</radical> radical. A bit creepy, but imagine how easily you could grip something or scratch your back with fingery fingers like these. Pretty nice, right?

This is also a lot like the hand radical (手) but smaller. And what are the smaller parts of a hand? The fingers! You can remember it that way too, if you want.

Take a good look at this one. It kind of looks like a <radical>heart</radical>. Not the heart emoji kind, but a real-deal beating heart. Basically, there's a lump in the middle (the heart), and three lines that make up the arteries. Okay, so it's not the most anatomically correct heart, but just look at those floppy arteries going in and out, doing their thing and keeping you alive. What's not to love?
This radical looks like a dude running off to the right. He's heading in a very distinct <radical>direction</radical>. Which direction was it again?
Do you remember the hair radical? This is like that, except now the hair is attached to a tail. Animals don't usually have hair though. Instead, they have <radical>fur</radical>.

This is the <radical>father</radical> radical, since you can see a very fatherly face in it — two droopy eyes at the top, a big nose in the middle, and a mustache flaring out at the bottom. Sort of a generic older gentleman father-type face, isn't it?

Put a cross over the mouth of a container full of all the <radical>old</radical> things you no longer need. They've all served their purpose but have gotten old, so it's now time to let them rest in peace under the cross. Goodbye, old things!
See the <radical>drawer</radical>? It has two shelves in it with a little nubbin handle on each to let you pull them out. Imagine using this drawer - it'd be pretty oddly shaped.

This looks like a little whiteboard to keep track of your <radical>task</radical>s for the day. It's got three little legs on the bottom. And see those blank squares? They're sticky notes you can write your tasks on. Work tasks, school tasks, WaniKani reviews… So what are your tasks for today? Imagine putting them in those little squares.

This is a gun on top of a big person. The gun is big too, obviously. Why is this big guy's gun so big? Because it shoots <radical>arrow</radical>s! Bullets are pretty small, so the guns that shoot them can be any size. But you need a big gun if you want to shoot a big arrow, right? That's why this is the radical for arrow.

This one looks like a flag, but don't be fooled — it's got a line over the top of it, kind of like a door frame. That makes this a little <radical>door</radical>. Specifically a swinging door, with the vertical line on the left being its door hinge. Kind of a weird door, it's true, but you can see it, right?
This is a <radical>roof</radical> ー a flat roof with a little chimney sticking out. How cute!

For better or worse, this looks enough like the poop emoji (💩) to make this the <radical>poop</radical> radical. Try to remember it for its distinct outline. If it helps you can also note the private radical on the bottom of this one, since you should probably be in private when you poop…

There's something draped over that stick. It's a <radical>towel</radical>! It's the kind of towel you clean with, so it's sort of old and crusty, which is why it holds its square shape even when it's hanging on the stick like that.

See the criss-cross in the almost-square shape? That's the frames of a big <radical>window</radical> you can look out of. It's not perfectly shaped like a rice field, it's more artistic. That's why this is a window and 田 is not.

Remember the radical for drop (of liquid)? Looks like it's shattered into two pieces here, which means it must be <radical>ice</radical> now. You know, since a drop could only break in two after turning into ice.

Remember the sprout from the dirt radical? This looks like that, but wait a minute… there's some extra growth now! This thing is so full of <radical>life</radical>! It's even got a big, slide-shaped leaf growing on the top left. That's why it's the life radical.

This is the radical for <radical>now</radical>. It's a bit tough to see, but it kind of looks like a fancy clock. The 𠆢 is the top part hanging over the clock. The ラ shows a triangular clock face with a little cuckoo on top, peeking out to tell you this means now — right now!

You only have some ice and a stick for your spoon, because you're way up north. At the top of the world, there's only ice to eat, and — if you're lucky — a bit of stick for flavor. That's the <radical>north</radical> for you.
The sun AND the moon are out? With both their light-powers combined, it's incredibly <radical>bright</radical> outside.

This looks like the guy from the big radical, but he's got something extra on his belly. That's his exposed belly button, because he's a sumo wrestler now: big and <radical>fat</radical>. In sumo, more fat means more power, so imagine he's been training to get as strong and fat as possible.
Do you know those rice paddy hats? The ones shaped just like this radical? That's why this radical is a <radical>hat</radical>.
The three horns represent the <radical>triceratops</radical>, one of the most awesome dinosaurs ever.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Under the <radical>ground</radical>, there's a <radical>prison</radical> with <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> inmates.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture ten thousand inmates crammed into this underground prison. Then, imagine yourself as the warden doing a head count to make sure all ten thousand of them are present.
kanji.readingMnemonic: To entertain the inmates, the prison is stocked with <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> volumes of <reading>man</reading>ga (まん).
kanji.readingHint: As the warden, you need to select all ten thousand of these manga volumes yourself. Which manga will you choose? Better start drafting your top 10,000 manga list now.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>now</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>now</kanji> as well.
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Right <kanji>now</kanji> the <reading>con</reading>dors (こん) are in danger! Not next week, not next year, right now! Haven't you heard that deforestation and pollution are killing all of the condors?!
kanji.readingHint: Go outside right now and do something to save the condors. If you don't do something right now there won't be enough time left!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>fins</radical> that fell onto my <radical>sword</radical> were sliced into many <kanji>part</kanji>s. Following this logic, this also means <kanji>minute</kanji>, which is part of an hour, and <kanji>divide</kanji>, which is the action of splitting something into many parts.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the fins falling onto the sword, and being divided into many parts. And if those fins represented hours, they’d be divided into minutes. Makes sense, right?
kanji.readingMnemonic: Now that the fins have been cut into neat <kanji>part</kanji>s, it's time to cut something else: <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん).
kanji.readingHint: This is how you feed your people: neatly divided, delicious buns. Picture these delicious buns divided into perfectly shaped parts. Yummy.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you have <radical>seven</radical> <radical>swords</radical>, there's only so much you can do with them. The main thing? Probably using them to <kanji>cut</kanji> something.
kanji.meaningHint: Take these seven swords and swing them around. <kanji>Cut</kanji> everything in your path, including yourself. Then, think about how dumb it was to try to use seven swords at once, and then feel the pain of the cut you gave yourself. Ouch, ouch ouch.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Because having seven swords for yourself is too much, you decide to take the swords and divide them up amongst pairs of people. You <kanji>cut</kanji> them into pairs, and give <reading>sets</reading> (せつ) to everyone who needs them in the village.
kanji.readingHint: Just make sure you think about how you need to give them away in <reading>sets</reading>, and not anything else. This is the most important thing to think about in your head as you're trying to establish the mnemonic for your kanji reading memory. It's gotta be sets.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>slide</radical> is <radical>dry</radical> at <kanji>noon</kanji>. The sun is brightest at noon, so it dries the morning dew off the slide, making noon the perfect time to slide.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all the kids out sliding on the slide at noon during their lunch break. It's hot and dry and they're very happy.
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>Noon</kanji> also happens to be the time <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) decided to attack for the same reasons: it's dry and kids are using the slide.
kanji.readingHint: Watch in horror as Godzilla's giant foot crushes all the kids and their slide at exactly noon. You'd better go...

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>narwhal</radical> sitting on a <radical>stool</radical> is your <kanji>friend</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine that narwhal sitting there. It waves its flipper and says "hi friend" to you.
kanji.readingMnemonic: "Hi <kanji>friend</kanji>," says the narwhal. "I must warn you about all the <reading>you</reading>ths." (ゆう)
kanji.readingHint: Your narwhal friend goes on to warn you about all those youths, and how they will try to take away your friendship with their good looks and young ages.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so this means <kanji>fat</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: We've fattened you up with lots of juicy radical knowledge, so this one should be pretty easy.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Imagine a <kanji>fat</kanji> person who loves to sleep on <reading>futo</reading>n (ふと).
kanji.readingHint: Picture this fat person curled up all cozy-like on their Japanese futon. They look so content! Have you ever slept on a proper Japanese futon, by the way? We're talking premium, cloud-grade comfort — luxurious enough to make you feel like a real fat cat.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>small</radical> <radical>slide</radical>. The thing about small slides is that <kanji>few</kanji> people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a small slide (how could you not, after you see the radicals?). So few people can use this thing, really, but there are a few little ones who can fit on it at least.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Another reason so <kanji>few</kanji> people can use it is that the <reading>Sho</reading>gun (しょう) is trying to go down the slide. We're talking a grown man who's way too big for this little slide, so a few people have to wait behind him — it's a slide traffic jam.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine this in your head. Even the few people who fit on the slide are struggling to get past the Shogun. Meanwhile the Japanese secret service is trying to make sure no one gets close to the shogun while he slides. A few people are crying. They want to slide, they want to leave… It's chaos.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you have a <radical>bow</radical> and a <radical>stick</radical> you need to <kanji>pull</kanji> the two back together to shoot it. If you can't pull it, you won't be shooting anything.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine taking a stick and pulling it back into your bow. Imagine how hard you have to pull. This thing is really strong!
kanji.readingMnemonic: When you <kanji>pull</kanji> the bow back, your body strains and you feel an immense <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) rise inside of you. You keep pulling and the heat grows hotter and hotter.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine using all your strength to pull on this bow. Imagine the heat rising in your body. There's sweat dripping down your face. It's so hot, but you have to keep pulling!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>heart</radical> and the kanji <kanji>heart</kanji> are the same. Rejoice and let your heart be free!
kanji.meaningHint: Also, make sure you know the radicals by heart, it'll help you to learn more effectively, just like with this kanji.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>heart</kanji>, where is it stored in your body? Most people thought it was in the chest, but in reality, your <kanji>heart</kanji> is stored in your <reading>shin</reading> (しん).
kanji.readingHint: This is when I start kicking you in the shin and you imagine feeling the pain of getting kicked there. As I kick you in the shin, the stress is getting too much for your poor heart inside your shin. Poor shin, and poor heart.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for <kanji>door</kanji> are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Time to open the door to the reading part of this mnemonic.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You open the <kanji>door</kanji> and immediately get it closed back on your <reading>toe</reading> (と), literally causing your toe to explode.
kanji.readingHint: Feel the pain of your toe going away. Think about the other side of the <kanji>door</kanji>, where your <reading>toe</reading> is probably rolling around after it blasted off your foot.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The radical and the kanji for <kanji>direction</kanji> are the same! Huzzah!

There is also another meaning too, though. This can also mean <kanji>way</kanji> as well. Think of it this way: When you move in one direction in your life, you are developing your own way. "The way of [your name here]."
kanji.meaningHint: The only direction you need to go in is forward, it's always the right way.
kanji.readingMnemonic: What <kanji>direction</kanji> do you always know? Which direction do you always want to go? <reading>Ho</reading>me (ほう). Something about your home always stays with you, no matter how far away you go. So if you're lost and you don't know which direction to go, just think of home!
kanji.readingHint: Close your eyes and picture your home in your mind. Can you tell which direction it is from where you are?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for <kanji>cow</kanji> are exactly the same! That makes it easy to remember, so long as you know your radicals well enough.
kanji.meaningHint: To distinguish this from the "noon" kanji (午), try thinking of the bit poking out of the top of this kanji as a tuft of hair on the cow's head — a cow lick, if you like.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Have you ever heard of わ<reading>ぎゅう</reading> (wagyu) beef? That ぎゅう is this ぎゅう.
kanji.readingHint: I hope you know what わぎゅう beef is, otherwise this will be a difficult one to learn.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for <kanji>father</kanji> are the same.
kanji.meaningHint: No, I am not your father... but this kanji / radical set is!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Imagine your father is <reading>Cheech</reading> (ちち) from Cheech and Chong.
kanji.readingHint: Hopefully you know who they are. If not, think about your father laughing like this: ちちちちちちちち〜！

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Fur</kanji> and <radical>fur</radical> are the same as each other, so the meaning of this kanji should be simple. This can also mean <kanji>hair</kanji>, too, though more like furry hair.
kanji.meaningHint: Just make sure you're studying your radicals, otherwise it won't be as simple as I'd hoped.
kanji.readingMnemonic: With <kanji>fur</kanji>, whisk your imagination to a land where there are stalks of fur all around, just like a big tall grassy field (except instead of grass, it's fur). You're surrounded by the black fur, the wind is blowing. Imagine yourself touching the long fur and smelling it. What does it feel and smell like? Now it's time to get rid of it. There's just too much <kanji>hair</kanji>! To get rid of it, you'll need to <reading>mow</reading> (もう) it down with a lawn mower. Imagine yourself starting up the lawn mower, and taking it around, mowing down the hair. Hear the sound of the mower in your head (they're loud and distinct). The important thing is to imagine yourself mowing everything. Key is to think "fur → in the fur → get rid of the fur → mow the fur," in that order. That'll get you to "mow," which will help you to remember the on’yomi.
kanji.readingHint: Smell the <kanji>fur</kanji> as you <reading>mow</reading> it down. Feel it flying everywhere. It's giant, so it must be pretty intense. Make it more intense to help yourself to remember the reading of this kanji better.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>stop</radical> radical is the same as the <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji.
kanji.meaningHint: Know your radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You have to <kanji>stop</kanji> because there is a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) in front of you. You try to walk around the sheep, but it moves to stop in front of you again. Every time the sheep stops you stop too.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the fluffy wool of the sheep, stopping you from moving forward. You can't push past it, no matter how hard you try.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You’ve got a <radical>winter</radical> with lots of <radical>ice</radical>. But doesn't any winter have lots of ice? Exactly. That's why this is just <kanji>winter</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: You go outside. There's ice everywhere. It's freezing cold. Yep, this is definitely winter.
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>Winter</kanji> is also the time of year you give out presents: "One fu' you, one fu' you and… one <reading>fu' you</reading> (ふゆ)!"
kanji.readingHint: Your pronunciation might be a little weird. But that’s okay. People still love your presents, and the way you say "fu’ you!"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical — it means <kanji>north</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Hold on to that radical knowledge! It'll be the north star that guides you through your studies.
kanji.readingMnemonic: In the <kanji>north</kanji>, everyone has a <reading>keytar</reading> (きた) — you know, those keyboards that people hold and play like a guitar. It's probably because it's so cold in the north. Playing a regular guitar is practically impossible with gloves on, but a keytar? Totally doable.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a bunch of people with thick winter gloves on, jamming out on their keytars. This is the kind of scene you'll only see in the north.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>triceratops</radical> is lying out to <radical>dry</radical>. But it's so big, and it's lying on its side, so only <kanji>half</kanji> of it gets dry.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the triceratops on its side, then imagine it getting up. When it stands up normally, half of its body is soaking wet still. It's a half-n-half triceratops right now.
kanji.readingMnemonic: "You're half wet and half dry! I will cut you in <kanji>half</kanji> with my laser blaster so you're proper again," a voice says. It is  <reading>Han</reading> Solo (はん), the anti-establishment guy who hates when things aren't even.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine him using his blaster to shoot the poor triceratops in half, perfectly down the wet-dry line of its body.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>old</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>old</kanji> as well.

Note: This "old" does not refer to people. Think of it as "old things" instead.
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic:
<kanji>Old</kanji> things are misunderstood by the <reading>子</reading>s (こ) of the world.

*Note:* Come up with a 子 character you can use for all the こ reading mnemonics going forward. This child will show up many times throughout your mnemonic journey, and it will help if you imagine the same character the whole time.
kanji.readingHint:
Imagine a 子 looking at old things. A record player. A Game Boy. A cassette player. Kids just don't get old things.

Note: When you see the (古) radical in a kanji, there's a good chance it will use the reading こ.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>private</radical> <radical>mouth</radical> that's a <kanji>machine</kanji>. But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you.
kanji.meaningHint: Doesn't this kanji look like a machine mouth? Now wouldn't you want to keep that private from the people you know?
kanji.readingMnemonic: To make sure they can't tell what's <kanji>machine</kanji> and what's human, you <reading>dye</reading> (だい) the mouth to make it look like skin. You find dye the same shade as your normal mouth and just slap it on there.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine being so afraid that people will find out about your machine mouth that you have to dye it to match a normal human mouth. Oh, when will this discrimination against machine-kind end?!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're known to get the ailment <radical>evening</radical> <radical>toe</radical>, which is when your toe catches on fire after getting really, really hot (imagine this happening, ouch!). The only way to fix it is to cool your toe down, and the best way to do that is to go <kanji>outside</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: After imagining your evening toe overheating, rush outside to fix it. It's the best way to prevent fire toe, which is way worse. In the evening it's nice and cold outside too, so feel this on your skin, and feel the cold air on your toe, which is starting to get some relief.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You go <kanji>outside</kanji> (you're not supposed to be out there at night!) and you're accosted by a couple of guys. Then, all of a sudden, <reading>Guy</reading> (がい) Fawkes jumps from the roof above you and takes them out, then starts running. "Guy Fawkes!" you yell after him!
kanji.readingHint: If you don't know Guy Fawkes, you should do a little reading up on him to make this mnemonic make sense. Also, Anonymous People wear a Guy Fawkes mask, if that helps any.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You see a manhole <radical>lid</radical> and a <radical>towel</radical>, both with the name of a <kanji>city</kanji> on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture this towel with the name of a city on it. Any city you like. Maybe it's your city!
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>city</kanji> must have a lot of <reading>shee</reading>p (し) because, besides the manhole lid and the towel, all you can see are sheep. There are sheep everywhere. It's a sheep city.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a city that has a sheep everywhere you look, as far as the eye can see. This city was built on sheep, don't you say a bad word about sheep when you're there.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>canopy</radical> you use in <radical>private</radical> is very <kanji>wide</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: You want your private canopy to be wide so you can sprawl out under it as much as you want. No one's going to come in and tell you to close your legs or sit up straight. So it can be as wide as you like!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You like being <kanji>wide</kanji> because it makes you feel like a different person. But not just any person, like a super <reading>hero</reading> (ひろ)!
kanji.readingHint: Picture yourself lying under your wide, private canopy pretending to be a super hero on the ground. You're stretching a nice, wide super hero pose, like you're flying through the sky.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Someone breaks part of your <radical>window</radical>. Who did this? It was your <kanji>mother</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: See how the vertical bar is broken and your window frame is all messed up now? Why would your mother do such a thing?! Her hand is bleeding too…
kanji.readingMnemonic: Suddenly your <kanji>mother</kanji> points her bloodied finger at you and laughs, "<reading>Haha</reading> (はは)!" She keeps laughing, haha haha haha, over and over. You feel even more alarmed.
kanji.readingHint:
You thought your mother was going to explain or apologize, but instead she's pointing and saying, "Haha," over and over.

Yeah. That sounds like my mom.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for <radical>task</radical> first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means <kanji>task</kanji> as well.
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Today, your <kanji>task</kanji> is to eat <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). It's nutritious, it's delicious, and I'm telling you to do it, so you have to. A task is basically just something you have to do, so that's what this is.
kanji.readingHint: Eat your yogurt. (Gogurt doesn't count, don't @ me.)

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>arrow</radical> radical and the <kanji>arrow</kanji> kanji are the same. Sort of a "straight" shot to memorizing this kanji, you know?
kanji.meaningHint: Just know your radicals and you'll know this kanji!
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember the reading や we use the word “Yankees” (like the evil baseball team, go M’s!).

What is this arrow doing? It’s following around all the <reading>Ya</reading>nkee (や) baseball players, stalking them, waiting to make its move (I’ll let you decide what its “move” is).
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the arrow as a human-sized living thing with legs, arms, and clothes, though. Strangely, it’s able to walk around even though it's an arrow. It has some kind of agenda. Make it a bit evil, if you can. What a strange thing…

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>roof</radical> <radical>child</radical> stands upon the roof, holding up a single <kanji>letter</kanji>, a single <kanji>character</kanji>, a single <kanji>symbol</kanji> for the world to see.
kanji.meaningHint: More people can see this character since the kid is on the roof.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>character</kanji> that is being shown is "J," which stands for <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ). The kid wants everyone to see this <kanji>letter</kanji> and <kanji>symbol</kanji>.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the child holding up the letter yelling at everyone who passes that the "J" stands for "Jesus." And yes, this kid just loves the Big Lebowski.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>bright</radical> radical and the <kanji>bright</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: If you already know the radical, this one's a freebie. That should make your day a little brighter, hm?
kanji.readingMnemonic: What do you say when you see something <kanji>bright</kanji>? "<reading>Ah</reading> (あ)!" Like when you open the curtain and the sunshine hits your eyes, or someone shines a flashlight right into your face. Ahhhh, so bright!
kanji.readingHint: You might also say "Ah!" when you come up with a bright idea, like in those light bulb moments.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>life</radical> radical and the <kanji>life</kanji> kanji are the same, so hopefully you now just know them both.
kanji.meaningHint: Study your radicals and you'll read good.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You can save <kanji>life</kanji> or take it away with your new <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). This is the saber you got from doing the correct thing (remember?), and now you need to figure out how to use it with this life. So what do you do?
kanji.readingHint: Imagine having someone's life in the palm of your hands. It's up to you whether you protect it with your saber or... well... do the other thing sabers are for.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The アメリカ part is pretty easy so long as you know katakana. It's the word for "America." You know that <kanji>人</kanji> means "person," so you can figure out that America + Person = <vocabulary>American person</vocabulary> — specifically a <vocabulary>person from the USA</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

<vocabulary>Americans</vocabulary> absolutely love their <reading>jean</reading>s (じん), it's a well-known fact!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: フランス is "France." So what is a "France person?" That would be a <vocabulary>French person</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん. Like people of all other nationalities, a <vocabulary>French person</vocabulary> loves their <reading>jean</reading>s (じん) too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you see a katakana word, it's a safe bet that it is a foreign loan word from somewhere else. This one's interesting, because it combines katakana and kanji! The first <vocabulary>marble</vocabulary> came to Japan from Portugal, so the ビー part of the word is short for "vidro," which means "glass" in Portuguese. Anyway, don't get thrown off by that ビー. Maybe just imagine that your favorite marble is black and yellow like a bee.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: If you know katakana as well as the reading that you learned when you learned the kanji <kanji>玉</kanji>, you should be able to read this. Just watch out for the rendaku.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Since this is a kanji with hiragana attached that ends with an う sound, you know that this word is a verb. What's the ultimate verb version of the kanji 生? That would be <vocabulary>to be born</vocabulary>, the very beginning of <kanji>life</kanji> as we know it!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
You have to remember the う part of this word to read it. To remember that, let's use a mnemonic: 

Something is about to be born, and when you lean in for a closer look… it’s an <reading>u</reading>ni (う). Yes, a sea urchin. You weren’t expecting that. Close your eyes and imagine what the process of an uni being born might look like, to help you remember this reading.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Normally a single kanji alone like this would mean the same thing as its parent kanji, but in the case of <kanji>生</kanji> it's a little different (but still related). When you think of something that has life, it's <vocabulary>fresh</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>raw</vocabulary>. Think sashimi or sushi, for example. You want that to be as close as possible to life as you can, so you eat it when it's fresh and raw. This word can also be used to describe a <vocabulary>live</vocabulary> event, like a concert or sporting event. 

You'll see this word at the beginning of other words. For example, 生たまご is "raw egg."
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This uses one of the kun'yomi readings. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

After eating <vocabulary>raw</vocabulary> fish, my yoga teacher and I say <reading>nama</reading>ste (なま) to the sushi chef, bowing low to show our appreciation.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you have <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> you just have <vocabulary>ten thousand</vocabulary>. In Japanese, though, you specify how many ten thousands you have (which is weird in English, but should make sense if you think about it).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you have <kanji>two</kanji> <kanji>ten thousand</kanji>s, you have <vocabulary>twenty thousand</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Ten</kanji> <kanji>ten thousand</kanji>s is equal to <vocabulary>one hundred thousand</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

What'll you drink now? I'll have a Zima, <reading>ima</reading>.

Say "ZIMA IMA" ten times fast.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> is what day? Oh, it's <vocabulary>today</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading for this word is a complete exception, though the word itself is incredibly common and useful. When you think of "today" think about what you have to do <vocabulary>today</vocabulary> for work.

You have to work in one of those mall <reading>kio</reading>sks (きょう). Just think about how sad you are that you have to do this today. What a crummy day. It's sunny outside and you're stuck in a mall manning this hermit crab kiosk.

Note: This reading mnemonic is pretty far away from the actual reading, as far as reading mnemonics go. Use this to get yourself close, and then use your own brain grapes to get the rest of the way there. This one won't be as easy as most of the others, but do some good old fashioned memorization and you should be okay. I won't ask you to do this much, fortunately. :)

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> <kanji>month</kanji> is actually <vocabulary>this month</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but since this is NOT a specific month name, it's going to use the げつ reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that:

Only <vocabulary>this month</vocabulary>, your pet <reading>con</reading>dor <reading>gets</reading> (こんげつ) to sleep in your bed. You usually keep it in a cage, but once a year, you make an exception. And that's this month. How cute!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>half</kanji> a <kanji>part</kanji>. Half a part is still <vocabulary>half</vocabulary>, right?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word has the same meaning that you learned with the kanji: <vocabulary>part</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>portion</vocabulary>. By extension, it can also mean <vocabulary>content</vocabulary>, as in "alcohol content" because that's the portion of alcohol in a drink.

This word is used for fractions, too, as in one third or one quarter. Again, you can see how this links to "parts" and "portions", right?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word is usually combined with a word or phrase indicating whose part or portion you're referring to. That's probably why this single kanji vocab word uses the on'yomi instead of the kun'yomi reading. Check out the common word combinations to see what we're talking about!

And when it means <vocabulary>part</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>portion</vocabulary>, it's read ぶん. Probably because your buns come in two parts. Ohoho.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Think back to the old old olden days. Back when decisions were made with swords. A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>cut</kanji> is going to be <vocabulary>important</vocabulary>. Just imagine a couple samurai squaring off, then charging, then making one big cut. It's the most important thing they'll do in their lives (if they live!).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

It's extremely <vocabulary>important</vocabulary> to keep your <reading>tie</reading>s in <reading>sets</reading> (たいせつ). If you don't arrange them neatly in sets, the tie police might just come knocking at your door and take you with them!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>cut</kanji>, and the verb form of that is <vocabulary>to cut</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: When you think <vocabulary>to cut</vocabulary> something, what do you think about cutting? One thing is cutting down a tree, which is also known as <reading>木</reading> (き). You 切る a 木.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A person who is a friend is just that, a <vocabulary>friend</vocabulary>!

Note that 友人 is a more formal word that’s often used in professional settings.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

All your <vocabulary>friend</vocabulary>s are <reading>you</reading>ths in <reading>jean</reading>s (ゆうじん)! Every single one. If any of your friends is not a youth in jeans, they're simply not your friend, I'm afraid.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of the <kanji>fat</kanji>? It's the same: <vocabulary>fat</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is the kun'yomi reading of the kanji (because it's a single kanji, all alone with hiragana attached). You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go. But here's a mnemonic just in case:

The <vocabulary>fat</vocabulary> cat loves to curl up on the <reading>futo</reading>n (ふと) all day.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word is a single kanji with hiragana attached, though there is no specific clue as to what type of word it is. That means you can usually guess it's a noun, adverb or na-adjective (in this case it's a noun / adverb). The meaning of this word is pretty much the same as the kanji, though, making it fairly easy. The kanji meaning for <kanji>少</kanji> is <kanji>few</kanji>, and the meaning of the vocab form is <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>a few</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Did you know that this word created an English word you probably already know? Have you ever heard someone say "just a skosh"? That's <vocabulary>少し</vocabulary>! Hopefully you know this English word and therefore know this Japanese word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word has a single kanji with hiragana attached, ending in a い. This means you know it's an adjective. What is the adjective form of <kanji>few</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>few</vocabulary>, as in <vocabulary>not much</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>not many</vocabulary> of something.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading for this one is fairly difficult, as it's the kun'yomi reading (you can tell it's kun'yomi because of all the hiragana attached). You have to remember the すく part to remember the reading of this word. Think of it this way:

You live in an area with very <vocabulary>few</vocabulary> <reading>schoo</reading>ls (すく). Maybe you're in rural Japan, where schools decrease year by year due to the shrinking population. Since there are so few schools now, you have to commute to the next town over to get an education. It's a little inconvenient, but hey — a few schools is better than no schools.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pull</kanji> and the verb version vocab means <vocabulary>to pull</vocabulary>.

This word can be transitive or intransitive. You use 引く in a transitive way to say you pull something, for example. But it can also mean <vocabulary>to withdraw</vocabulary> when you talk about things that pull back, like water that recedes, pain that subsides, soldiers that withdraw, or even your body recoiling when something puts you off.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. The reading (ひ) is the same as the one you learned for the kanji, meaning you should already know it!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Imagine a giant <vocabulary>heart</vocabulary> sitting in a rowing boat. It's also drinking cocoa. Focus on all three of these parts and associate them into one story / memory. Once you've done that, sing the "<reading>cocoa row</reading>" (こころ) song! I don't know what that song is, but I want you to make one up and actually sing it, out loud. If you do, I bet you won't forget this word's reading too easily.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>door</kanji>'s <kanji>mouth</kanji> is the <vocabulary>doorway</vocabulary>! 

戸口 is mostly used for doorways that lead outside. It has an old-fashioned feel to it and is becoming less common these days, especially in spoken Japanese.

You might notice that this word resembles 出口 (exit) and 入り口 (entrance). Like in those words, the character 口 just represents an opening here.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is mixed. You get the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, even though it's a combo (jukugo) kanji. Since 戸's only reading is the kun'yomi reading you should know it. Also, you should know the kun'yomi reading for 口 as well from level 1. That means as long as you remember that this is a kun'yomi fest over here, you should be able to read this word. Also watch out for the rendaku (also known as sequential voicing). That just means the く becomes the voiced ぐ.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

You learned 方 means <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary>, but it can also mean <vocabulary>way</vocabulary>, as in この方がいい (this <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> is better) or やり方 (the <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> of doing something). 

Interestingly, 方 can also be used to refer to people politely, like こちらの方 (this person). This is because, in traditional Japanese, people—especially noble ones—were often referred to indirectly, as if indicating their presence from a direction.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading, but it can actually use kun'yomi or on'yomi depending on the context. Here are a couple mnemonics to help you remember both readings and how they're most often used:

You can always remember which <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary> your <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう) is in. It's in こっちの方 (this direction)!

And the best <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> to get there is with a <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた). Just climb in the catapult and launch yourself there — it's the best やり方.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stop</kanji>, so the verb vocab version of that is <vocabulary>to stop something</vocabulary>. Alternatively, it can also mean <vocabulary>to stop doing something</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This word has two different readings for its slightly different meanings, so here's a couple mnemonics to help remember which is which:

When you need <vocabulary>to stop something</vocabulary> from moving, you use your <reading>toe</reading> (と). For most people, this would just lead to a stubbed toe, but you have toes of iron — sturdy enough to stop even speeding locomotives in their tracks.

On the other hand, when you need <vocabulary>to stop doing something</vocabulary> — you know, a bad habit or whatnot — you call over the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や). Imagine the whole New York Yankees squad cheering you on (or threatening you with their bats). You'd be able to quit immediately.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You're in the <kanji>middle</kanji> of something when someone yells "<kanji>stop</kanji>!" They hit you with a <vocabulary>cancellation</vocabulary> order and demand the immediate <vocabulary>discontinuation</vocabulary> of all your activities. Welp, it looks like you've been canceled — better go find something else to do.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Look down! You're holding something covered in <vocabulary>fur</vocabulary>. It's a furry <reading>ke</reading>ttle (け)! It's the weirdest kettle you've ever seen, but presumably it keeps the water hot for much longer.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is the polite and humble form of <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>. You use this when you're talking about your own <vocabulary>dad</vocabulary> to other people in formal settings, especially if you aren't very close to them.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word begins with an honorific (お), making whatever comes after it more elevated. Then there's 父, which you know means <kanji>father</kanji>. Lastly, we have the honorific name-ender <ja>さん</ja>. So this is a nice way to say <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>. 

You'll want to use this when you're addressing or calling out to your own <vocabulary>dad</vocabulary>, or when you're talking about him or someone else's dad in a casual setting.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The part you have to learn to read is the 父 portion. It uses the kun'yomi, but not the one you initially learned with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this new reading:

The thing your <vocabulary>father</vocabulary> loves the most is <reading>とう</reading>きょう. He will not stop talking about とうきょう to you, and you just have to listen. とうきょう this, とうきょう that. To really get this picture in your head, make sure to imagine your dad incessantly droning on about とうきょう.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are the same. This word is a bit broader than <vocabulary>cow</vocabulary> though, and can also be used to be <vocabulary>bull</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>ox</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

You're leading the cows around the field. To get them to move, you yell out "<reading>USH</reading>, USH, USH!" (うし) because you have a speech impediment and want to say "MUSH MUSH MUSH." Go ahead and say this out loud, yelling it if you can.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the kun'yomi reading you learned for the kanji, meaning you should know both!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You already learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it's supposed to use the kun'yomi reading. But, there is no useful kun'yomi reading for this kanji, so even the single kanji vocab word version uses the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>old</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>old</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>ancient</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>out-of-date</vocabulary>.

This word is used for things like clothes, food and friendships, but not for people! So a 古い友人 (old friend) is someone you've been friends with for a long time, not an elderly friend.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji with some hiragana attached, it's going to use the kun'yomi reading. You learned the on'yomi when learning the kanji portion, so let's use a mnemonic to help you with the reading of this word: 

If you're <vocabulary>old</vocabulary>, you're also <reading>full</reading> (ふる) of memories. And you're probably full of old secrets. And you're full from old people food.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The combination of kanji doesn't make perfect sense, but it's alright. Take something that's <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>old</kanji> and you have something that's <vocabulary>used</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>secondhand</vocabulary>. It's not 100% old yet... it's still in the middle, meaning you can give it to someone else to use, like your younger siblings.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: As long as you know the two kanji that make up this word, you should be able to figure out the meaning of this word as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you combine these two kanji, you should be able to see how it forms the word <vocabulary>two machines</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: As long as you know both of the individual kanji meanings, you should be able to put together this one to get <vocabulary>five machines</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you know the two kanji separately, you should be able to put them together to form the meaning of this kanji.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Note that 外 doesn't always simply indicate the physical position of something. It can also be used figuratively to refer to what's outside of one's inner circle or home.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You look <vocabulary>outside</vocabulary>, it's totally frozen. You throw <reading>salt</reading> (そと) outside to melt the ice.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: An "outside person" is a <vocabulary>foreigner</vocabulary>. This word is fairly common, though it's not super polite, either. It's okay most of the time, but it can be used derogatorily depending on the situation. The more polite version is 外国人 (outside country person) but you won't learn that until you learn the kanji for 国.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Who's the <vocabulary>foreigner</vocabulary>? Well obviously the <reading>guy</reading> wearing <reading>jean</reading>s (がいじん)!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When the <kanji>city</kanji> <kanji>stand</kanji>s something up, that thing becomes <vocabulary>municipal</vocabulary>. You know, like a <vocabulary>city-run</vocabulary> library or a city-run gym or something. The city is what keeps that place standing.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The name of the city (シアトル／しあとる) with a <kanji>市</kanji> attached to it means it is "the city of ____." You can do this with any city (try it out on your hometown!). So this word means <vocabulary>Seattle</vocabulary>, or more specifically <vocabulary>City of Seattle</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses on'yomi reading, which you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>wide</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>wide</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the reading you learned in the kanji section: ひろ, making this <reading>ひろ</reading>い.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they both mean mother. 母 is a formal and humble way to say "my mother" when talking to others. By using the plain form and omitting respectful language toward your own mom, you actually sound more humble, which makes a polite impression on the person you're speaking to. You wouldn't, however, use it when talking to your mom or when talking about someone else's mom — it would come off as too blunt for that!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but this is the reading you learned with the kanji. Just remember, your <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary> is a terrible person and won't stop laughing at you: "<reading>HA HA</reading>! HA HA!”

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word begins with an honorific (お), which generally adds a nuance of respect or politeness to what comes after it. Then there's 母, which you know means <kanji>mother</kanji>. Lastly, we have the honorific name-ender さん. So this is a nice way to say <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary>. You use it when talking about the <vocabulary>mom</vocabulary>s of friends or casual acquaintances, when talking about your own mom in a casual social setting, or when talking to your own mom.

In more formal settings, you'll want to use 母 (pronounced はは) to talk about your own mom and the super respectful お母さま to talk about someone else's mom.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You have to remember the かあ portion. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

What does your super nice <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary> do for you (this is why you're so polite to her!)? She drives you all around in her <reading>car</reading> (かあ) taking you wherever you need to go... soccer, kendo, whatever. What a nice mother you have!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>task</kanji> or <kanji>use</kanji>. You can think of this verb as a more formal way to say <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary>, and that is <vocabulary>to utilize</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to learn the もち portion of もちいる: 

What will you <vocabulary>utilize</vocabulary> to get the job done? You have <reading>mochi</reading> (もち) in your hand, so you'll use that. Now go think of some kind of imaginary task you'll complete with mochi, making it as ridiculous as possible.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You only learned one reading for the kanji that makes up this word, and it's the same as the reading for this word (of course). That means you should already know the reading.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji for <kanji>person</kanji> and <kanji>life</kanji> combined makes you think about human life. What is your <vocabulary>human life</vocabulary> like?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 and 生 both have two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your <vocabulary>life</vocabulary> boils down to just two things: <reading>jean</reading>s and a <reading>sa</reading>ber (じんせい). Your whole life, that's all you've ever needed, jeans and a saber. What are you, some kind of American pirate?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: イギリス means "Great Britain" or "United Kingdom." So what is a "Great Britain person?" You guessed it — a <vocabulary>British person</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>Brit</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん. All nationalities, including <vocabulary>Brit</vocabulary>s, love <reading>jean</reading>s (じん)!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This counter is used with some kind of <kanji>machine</kanji> or device, usually a fairly large one (so nothing itty bitty). Cars are a good example of this. But it can also be used for things like computers, which were once the size of rooms, but are now nice and small. Thanks technology!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to omit the 〜 in your answer as it is only a placeholder for a number.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you see this on a number, for example ７人 or ３人, you're using it to count people. Just remember, both 一人 and 二人 have alternative readings. From 3 and up it's just the number plus にん, like this. ５人 is ごにん, １０人 is じゅうにん, etc. This is the <vocabulary>counter for people</vocabulary>, which makes this word the <vocabulary>number of people</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a counter, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Just think of the sheer <vocabulary>number of people</vocabulary> at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (にん). It must be huge. This really is just a <vocabulary>counter for people</vocabulary> that work at Nintendo.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>few</kanji> <kanji>woman</kanji> — what's that? One with few years and few experiences, let's say, which means she's still a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>. 

少女 is a relatively formal word that's often used in writing to describe a <vocabulary>young girl</vocabulary>, usually between childhood and adolescence (or between the ages of about five and eighteen).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji without okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually has the same meaning as the kanji it's spawned from. If you know the kanji meaning you'll also know the vocab meaning. It's <vocabulary>ten thousand</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji with no okurigana, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception to this. Numbers use the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned by learning the kanji's reading! How nice!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This is a strange one. It's こんにちは, which you've probably heard before, but it's spelled using the kanji <kanji>now</kanji> and <kanji>day</kanji>. So when you say "now day!" you're really saying <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary>!

Warning! Don't mix this up with きょうは! While they may look the same, they don't mean the same thing. We will only ever ask you for こんにちは, so please try to remember that!

We usually don't use kanji for this, so don't use it when you're writing. But you'll probably run into it in the wild so it's good to know!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be aware that the は at the end is actually the particle は so it's pronounced like わ.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This one uses the on'yomi reading, which you've learned from the kanji already!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 大人 means "adult?" Well this is the adjective version of that. The I-adjective (see how it ends in い?). What adjective do adults want to be able to use for their own kids? They want to say they are <vocabulary>obedient</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary> kids!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You already learned this reading when you learned 大人! You should be able to read this too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>door</kanji> is a <vocabulary>door</vocabulary> — the kanji and the word are exactly the same.

戸 can refer to any kind of door, but it's more commonly used for <vocabulary>sliding door</vocabulary>s, since those are the traditional style of doors in Japan. For Western-style or high-tech doors, people tend to just say ドア.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>woman</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary>.

The の particle here means the first noun is modifying the second one, so you can probably see why 女の人 (a woman person) really just means woman! It's more polite than saying 女 by itself, so that's all you have to remember.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 1 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>wide</kanji>, and the verb version is what happens when you try to make something wider. How do you make something wider? That's right, you have <vocabulary>to spread something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to unfold something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to open something up</vocabulary>. All of those actions will make a thing wider!

This is a transitive verb. That means it takes a direct object. You spread something. Like a newspaper, or a cloth on a table.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a reminder mnemonic to help you:

You are going <vocabulary>to spread something</vocabulary>. What are you going to spread? How about your arms, so that you can fly into the sky like the super <reading>hero</reading> (ひろ) that you are! Most heroes can fly when they spread their arms wide!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You know that 山 means mountain. Add the hiragana びこ to the end and this gives you <vocabulary>echo</vocabulary>. That's because bee children (bee 子) love echos, especially <vocabulary>mountain echo</vocabulary>s! Imagine baby bees buzzing as loudly as they can and hearing their voices echoing back at them through the mountains.

As the kanji suggests, 山びこ is generally used to describe the echo you get if you shout in the mountains. To describe other types of echo, you can use the katakana word エコー.

By the way, there is actually a kanji for the second part of this word, but it's so rare that it's usually written in kana!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You learned this kanji reading when you learned the vocabulary 山.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: First we have a katakana word, so it's safe to assume that it's a loan word. Like many loan words, it comes from English. Say it out loud and what do you have? That's right, "table". Then comes the particle の, which joins two nouns together. Finally we have 上, which you learned means "up" or "above". Put all of these pieces together and we have a phrase meaning <vocabulary>on the table</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>tabletop</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: In this phrase, 上 is a standalone word, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary. Easy to stay on top of that one, right?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This starts with another katakana word, so you can assume that it's a loan word. This one also comes from English. Can you figure out what it means? That's right, "bed". Then comes the particle の, which joins two nouns together. Finally, we have 下, which you learned means "down" or "below". Put these elements together and you get <vocabulary>below the bed</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>under the bed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>beneath the bed</vocabulary>. What's under your bed?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: 下 is a standalone word here, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: What do we call the <kanji>sun</kanji>'s <kanji>exit</kanji> from the horizon? That'll be the <vocabulary>sunrise</vocabulary>. Imagine the sun exiting the horizon and climbing up into the sky.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This uses the kanji's kun'yomi readings, which you've already learned. As long as you remember those, you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You just learned the vocab 生, meaning fresh. Combined with the katakana word for beer makes this draft beer or unpasteurized beer.

Note that while in a lot of countries, "draft beer" refers only to beer that's drawn from a keg, 生ビール can also refer to unpasteurized canned or bottled beer, giving it a shorter shelf-life, but also keeping it fresh.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Be careful to use kun'yomi for 生 here. Other than that, as long as you know your katakana, you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how 入り口 means "entrance" and 出口 means "exit"? This vocab is just the 口 part with a direction added to it. This also makes it both an entrance or exit. So when you have the kanji for <kanji>north</kanji>, it makes this both a <vocabulary>north exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>north entrance</vocabulary>. This is a great word to know if you need to know which side of a train station you need to leave on to go somewhere or meet someone!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Just like 入り口 and 出口, this also uses kun'yomi readings. And just like before, watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
What makes it <kanji>bright</kanji> around here? It's <vocabulary>light</vocabulary>!

Note: 明かり is mostly used for light coming from a specific source, like a lamp or light bulb. You'll learn a more general word for light in a couple levels.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already know the reading from the kanji!
